unit.name: Data, Information and Networks
unit.subtitle: Making data fit for purpose, checking it for errors, and how networks move data.

lessons.title: Data, Information and Fit for Purpose
lessons.description: Explore what data and information mean, why quality matters, and how files are stored and compressed in ICT systems.
lessons.content_html:
Data, Information and Knowledge

When we talk about what computers work with, three terms come up again and again: data, information and knowledge. It is easy to muddle them, but they mean distinct things. Data consists of raw facts and figures. On their own they carry no meaning: the number 37 could be a temperature, a bus route or someone's age. Information is what we get when data has been processed by a computer to give it context — 37°C tells us it is a dangerously high body temperature. Knowledge takes things one step further: it is derived from information by applying rules. A doctor who knows that a temperature above 38°C in a newborn requires emergency hospital admission is applying knowledge — rules built on clinical information.

This hierarchy matters in ICT because computers process data to produce information, and well-designed systems encode the rules that turn information into actionable knowledge. When you type your date of birth into a form, you are providing raw data. The system processes it to tell you that you are 16 years old (information), and then applies a rule to decide whether you are old enough to create an account (knowledge in action).

Why Data Must Be Good Quality

For information to be useful, the data that feeds it must be fit for purpose. Good-quality data has several key characteristics. It must be accurate — if a patient's medication dosage is recorded incorrectly, the information produced from it could be dangerous. It must be complete — missing fields can make records unusable. It must be up to date — a customer address that was correct three years ago may have changed. It must also be relevant — collecting data that is never used wastes storage and processing resources. Poor-quality data leads to poor-quality information, which in turn leads to bad decisions. This is sometimes summed up as "garbage in, garbage out": if the raw data going into a system is wrong, no amount of processing will fix the output.

Key Fact

"Garbage in, garbage out" describes the reality that poor-quality data produces poor-quality information regardless of how powerful the computer is. The four key quality characteristics are: accuracy, completeness, currency (up to date) and relevance.

Encoding Data

Encoding is the process of converting data into a shorter or standardised form. For example, instead of storing the full word "Female", a database might store the single character "F". Instead of "Yes" or "No", a system might use 1 and 0. Encoding has clear benefits: it reduces the amount of storage space needed, speeds up sorting and searching because shorter codes are faster to compare, and reduces the chance of input errors because staff choose from a fixed set of codes rather than typing free text. However, encoding can also have disadvantages — codes may be misunderstood or misremembered, and they can make data harder for a non-expert to read without a reference key. There is also a risk that a code designed for one purpose becomes ambiguous over time as organisations grow and change.

Advances in ICT hardware have improved both the speed of access to data and the amount of storage available. Solid-state drives (SSDs) retrieve data far faster than older spinning hard drives. Cloud storage means an organisation is no longer limited by the physical capacity of the hardware on site. These improvements mean that organisations can store larger volumes of data and retrieve it more quickly, which directly improves the quality and timeliness of the information they produce.

Advantages and Disadvantages of Using ICT to Store Data

Storing data using ICT systems offers significant advantages. Large volumes of data can be searched in seconds — a task that would take days in a paper-based system. Data can be backed up automatically to prevent loss. Multiple authorised users can access the same records simultaneously from different locations. Data can be sorted, filtered and processed to create reports almost instantly. Despite these advantages, there are also real risks and drawbacks. Digital data is vulnerable to hacking, malware and unauthorised access. Hardware failure or software corruption can destroy records if backups are not in place. There are ongoing costs for hardware, software licences and security measures. Organisations also have legal obligations under data protection law when handling personal information digitally, and a breach can have serious financial and reputational consequences.

Key Fact

Key advantages of ICT data storage: fast search and retrieval, simultaneous multi-user access, automated backups, easy sorting and reporting. Key disadvantages: security vulnerabilities, hardware failure risk, ongoing costs, and legal compliance obligations.

File Types and File Properties

Not all files are the same. Different types of data are stored in different file formats. Common file types include: text files (.txt, .docx) for written documents; image files (.jpg, .png, .bmp) for photographs and graphics; audio files (.mp3, .wav) for sound; video files (.mp4, .avi) for moving images; and spreadsheet files (.xlsx, .csv) for numerical data. Each file type has different properties and is suited to different purposes. Choosing the wrong file type can reduce quality or cause compatibility problems.

Every file also has properties that describe it: its name, file type (extension), size (measured in bytes, kilobytes, megabytes or gigabytes), date created, date modified, and the author or owner. File size is particularly important in ICT because large files take longer to transfer over a network, require more storage space, and can slow down a system. Understanding file properties helps ICT users manage storage efficiently and choose the right format for their needs.

Data Compression

Data compression is the process of reducing a file's size. There are two main types. Lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data — when the file is decompressed it is identical to the original. ZIP files and PNG images use lossless compression. Lossy compression permanently removes data that is considered less important — the file is smaller but cannot be perfectly restored to its original state. JPEG images and MP3 audio files use lossy compression. The benefit of compression is faster file transfer over networks and less storage space used. The trade-off with lossy compression is reduced quality — though for many uses (streaming music, sharing photos online) the quality loss is not noticeable to most people.

With lossless compression (e.g. PNG, ZIP), no data is permanently removed — when you decompress the file it is bit-for-bit identical to the original. With lossy compression (e.g. JPEG, MP3), some data is permanently discarded. The algorithm decides which data is least perceptible to humans and throws it away. A JPEG photograph looks very similar to the original but is not identical — repeated saving of a JPEG degrades quality further each time. For professional photography or archiving legal documents, lossless formats are preferred. For web images and streaming audio where small quality reductions are acceptable, lossy formats save significant bandwidth and storage.

Consider a supermarket loyalty card database with 10 million customer records. Each record stores a "gender" field. If the system stores the full word "Male" or "Female" that is up to 6 characters per record, or 60 million characters across the database. Encoding it as "M" or "F" (1 character each) reduces this to 10 million characters — a 6× reduction for that field alone. When the database searches or sorts by gender, comparing a single character is faster than comparing six. Scale this across dozens of fields and millions of records and the efficiency gains are enormous. This is why encoding is standard practice in all large database-driven systems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions often ask you to distinguish data from information — always use the processing step in your answer ("data is processed by the computer to produce information"). For questions on advantages and disadvantages of ICT data storage, do not just list points: explain them with a brief "because" or "which means" to reach the higher mark bands. If asked to compare lossless and lossy compression, name an example file type for each (PNG / JPEG, or ZIP / MP3) — examiners reward specific examples and penalise vague answers that just say "one keeps quality and one doesn't".
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Data is raw facts and figures; information is data that has been processed by a computer to give it context; knowledge is derived from information by applying rules.
  • Good-quality data must be accurate, complete, up to date and relevant — poor data produces poor information ("garbage in, garbage out").
  • Encoding data (using short codes instead of full text) saves storage space, speeds up processing and reduces input errors.
  • ICT data storage offers advantages (speed, capacity, multi-user access) but also risks (security, cost, legal obligations).
  • Lossless compression reduces file size without losing data; lossy compression removes some data permanently to achieve greater size reduction.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes "information" in an ICT context?
A) Raw facts and figures entered into a computer system
B) Data that has been processed by a computer to give it context and meaning
C) Rules applied to data to reach a conclusion
D) A file stored on a hard drive
practice_questions.marks: B) Data that has been processed by a computer to give it context and meaning [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using ICT to store data compared with a paper-based system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct advantages from: fast search and retrieval / automated backups / simultaneous multi-user access / easy sorting and reporting / large storage capacity / data can be processed to produce reports. Answers that repeat the same idea score 1 mark only. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by encoding data and give one benefit of doing so.
practice_questions.marks: Encoding definition (up to 2 marks): converting data into a shorter or standardised representation, e.g. using M/F instead of Male/Female or 1/0 for Yes/No (2 marks for a clear definition with example; 1 mark for a basic definition without example). Benefit (1 mark): any one from — reduces storage space / speeds up searching and sorting / reduces input errors by limiting choices. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between lossless and lossy compression and give one example file type for each.
practice_questions.marks:
Lossless (2 marks): compression that reduces file size without permanently removing any data — the file is identical to the original when decompressed; example: PNG or ZIP (1 mark each, max 2 for lossless).
Lossy (2 marks): compression that permanently removes some data to achieve a greater reduction in file size — the file cannot be perfectly restored; example: JPEG or MP3 (1 mark each, max 2 for lossy). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: A school stores student records in a database. Give two characteristics of good-quality data and, for each, explain why that characteristic matters for this school database.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for naming a valid characteristic plus one mark for a relevant explanation, repeated for a second characteristic. For example: accuracy (1) — if a student's medical information is recorded incorrectly, the school may give the wrong first aid response in an emergency (1); up to date / currency (1) — if a home address is outdated, the school cannot contact parents in an emergency (1). Other valid characteristics: completeness, relevance. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small business is deciding whether to move from paper-based records to a digital ICT system for storing customer data.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using ICT to store data for this business, and recommend whether the move is worthwhile.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering multiple advantages (fast retrieval, large capacity, multi-user simultaneous access, automated backup, easy production of reports) and disadvantages (security risks including hacking and malware, ongoing costs for hardware/software/security, hardware failure risk, legal compliance obligations under data protection law, staff training needed). A substantiated recommendation is given — e.g. the move is worthwhile for a growing business because the efficiency gains outweigh the risks, provided security measures are implemented and staff are trained, but a very small business with few records and limited IT expertise might find the costs and risks disproportionate.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two advantages and two disadvantages, some developed, a recommendation attempted.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic relevant points with no development or recommendation. [8 marks]

Data that has been processed by a computer system to give it context and meaning, making it useful to a person or organisation.
Understanding derived from information by applying rules, experience or expertise to draw conclusions or make decisions.

lessons.title: Data Capture and Error Checking
lessons.description: How data is collected and how validation and verification techniques ensure accurate data entry.
lessons.content_html:
How Data Is Captured

Data capture refers to the methods and tools used to collect data and get it into a computer system. The method chosen has a big impact on accuracy, speed and cost. Manual methods include keyboard entry (typing data into a form or spreadsheet) and handwriting on paper forms that are later typed up. These methods are flexible but slow and prone to human error. Automated methods capture data without (or with minimal) human typing. A barcode scanner reads product codes at a supermarket checkout. A magnetic stripe or chip on a payment card is read by a card reader. Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software converts printed or handwritten text in a scanned image into editable digital text. Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) detects pencil marks in fixed positions on a form — used in multiple-choice exam answer sheets and lottery tickets. Sensors capture environmental data automatically: a temperature sensor on a weather station records readings every minute without any human involvement. Online forms with drop-down menus and checkboxes guide users toward valid entries, reducing errors compared to completely free-text entry.

No data capture method is perfect. Even automated systems can misread a damaged barcode or a smudged form. The data that enters a system must be checked for errors before it is stored or processed, otherwise the resulting information will be unreliable. Two distinct processes are used for this: validation and verification.

Validation

Validation is an automated check carried out by the computer to test whether data is reasonable and in the correct format. It is important to understand what validation cannot do: it cannot confirm that the data is factually true. For example, if a date-of-birth field expects a date in the past and a user types 01/01/2010, validation will accept it as a plausible date — even if the real date of birth is 01/01/2009. Validation simply checks that the data could be correct.

There are several types of validation check:

A range check confirms that a numeric value falls within acceptable limits. For instance, a student's exam mark out of 100 must be between 0 and 100 — the system would reject -5 or 150. A type check (also called a data type check) confirms that the data entered matches the expected data type for that field. A name field expects text; if a user enters numbers, the type check rejects the entry. A presence check ensures that a required field has not been left blank — useful for mandatory fields such as a customer's surname or email address. A format check (also called a picture check) verifies that the data matches a specific pattern. A UK postcode must follow a pattern such as SW1A 1AA; a date must follow DD/MM/YYYY. A length check confirms that the entry is within an acceptable number of characters — a mobile phone number in the UK should be 11 digits, so the system would reject an entry of 8 or 15 digits. Finally, a check digit is an extra digit added to a code (such as an ISBN book number or barcode) that is calculated mathematically from the other digits. When the code is entered, the system recalculates the check digit and compares it to the one entered — a mismatch reveals a keying error.

Key Fact

The six validation checks are: range check (value within limits), type check (correct data type), presence check (field not empty), format check (correct pattern), length check (correct number of characters), check digit (mathematical digit to spot keying errors).

Verification

Verification checks that data has been copied or transferred correctly from one place to another. Unlike validation, verification does not check whether the data is reasonable — it checks whether it has been faithfully reproduced. There are two main verification methods. Double entry (also called double keying) requires a user to type the data twice — the computer compares the two entries and flags any difference. This is commonly used when setting a new password: you type it once, then again to confirm. If the two entries do not match, you are asked to try again. Proof reading is a human review of data before it is confirmed — a member of staff reads through entered data and compares it against the original source document to spot any errors. This is less automated but can catch subtle mistakes that a computer might miss.

Key Fact

Validation = automated computer check that data is reasonable and in the right format. Verification = check that data has been accurately transferred or copied. Double entry and proof reading are the two main verification techniques.

Sources of Error

Errors can enter a system at multiple points. Transcription errors occur when data is copied from one place to another — a typist accidentally hits "8" instead of "9", or two adjacent characters are swapped (a transposition error). Transmission errors happen during the transfer of data over a network — interference or signal degradation can corrupt data in transit. Original source errors occur when the original data is simply wrong from the start — a customer gives an incorrect telephone number, or a sensor is miscalibrated. Data loss can occur during processing if a system crashes before data is saved. Deliberate falsification is where a person intentionally enters false information — for example, giving a false age on a website form. No single checking technique can prevent all of these errors, which is why systems combine multiple approaches.

Validation is appropriate when you know in advance what "reasonable" data looks like for a field. A date-of-birth field for a school student might have a range check (must be between 2003 and 2015) and a format check (DD/MM/YYYY). Verification is appropriate when data has been copied from a source document and you need to confirm the copy is accurate — for example, a data entry clerk typing patient records from paper forms. The two methods are complementary: a data entry system might validate each field as the clerk types, AND ask the clerk to proof read the final record against the paper form before clicking Submit. Together they dramatically reduce the rate of errors that reach the database.

A check digit is the final digit of a product barcode or ISBN, calculated mathematically from all the preceding digits using a set algorithm. For example, in an ISBN-13, each of the first 12 digits is multiplied alternately by 1 and 3, the results are summed, and the check digit is the number needed to make the total divisible by 10. When a barcode is scanned at a till, the system repeats this calculation on the first 12 digits. If the result matches the scanned check digit, the data is accepted. If there is a mismatch — caused, for example, by a scanning error or a damaged barcode — the system alerts the operator. Check digits are particularly effective at catching transposition errors (where two digits are accidentally swapped) because swapping changes the calculated total.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam mistake is to confuse validation and verification. Remember: validation is done by the computer and checks if the data is reasonable — it cannot tell you if the data is actually true. Verification checks that the data has been copied correctly. If the question gives you a scenario, identify which type of error is at risk: if data is being transferred or re-keyed, think verification; if the question asks whether entered values make sense, think validation. When naming a validation check, always name the specific type (range, type, presence, format, length or check digit) rather than just saying "the computer checks the data" — the specific type earns the mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Data capture methods include keyboard entry, barcode scanners, OCR, OMR, sensors and online forms — each with different accuracy and speed trade-offs.
  • Validation is an automated computer check that data is reasonable and in the correct format; it cannot confirm data is factually true.
  • The six types of validation check are: range, type, presence, format, length and check digit.
  • Verification confirms that data has been copied or transferred correctly; the two main methods are double entry and proof reading.
  • Sources of error include transcription errors, transmission errors, original source errors, data loss and deliberate falsification — no single technique prevents all of them.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a validation check?
A) A user types their password twice to confirm it matches
B) A staff member reads through a typed record against the original paper form
C) A system rejects a date of birth entered as 45/13/2010 because it is not a valid date format
D) A manager checks a printed report for errors before filing it
practice_questions.marks: C) A system rejects a date of birth entered as 45/13/2010 because it is not a valid date format [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two methods of automated data capture.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct automated methods from: barcode scanner / OCR (Optical Character Recognition) / OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) / magnetic stripe / chip reader / sensor / biometric scanner. Manual methods such as keyboard entry do not score. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between validation and verification in data entry.
practice_questions.marks: Validation (1 mark): an automated check by the computer that data is reasonable and in the correct format. Verification (1 mark): a check that data has been copied or transferred correctly from one place to another. Development / distinction (1 mark): a clear statement that validation cannot confirm data is factually true — it only checks plausibility — whereas verification confirms accuracy of transfer (e.g. double entry or proof reading). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school uses an online form to enrol new students. Describe two different validation checks that could be applied to a field that asks for the student's age.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for each validation check described: one mark for naming the check type and one mark for applying it to the age field. For example: range check (1) — the age field only accepts values between 11 and 18, rejecting any number outside this range (1); type check (1) — the field only accepts numeric characters, rejecting letters or symbols (1). Other valid pairs: presence check (field cannot be left blank) + length check (age cannot exceed 3 digits). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A hospital is transferring patient records from paper files to a new digital database. Identify two possible sources of error during this process and, for each, suggest a technique that could be used to reduce that error.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each error source identified, one mark for each appropriate technique. For example: transcription error when typing (1) — use double entry / proof reading (1); transmission error if records are emailed to the database team (1) — use parity checking or checksum to verify data arrived intact (1). Other valid pairs: original source error (paper record was wrong) — verify against original medical notes before entry; deliberate falsification — restrict access to authorised data entry staff. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A supermarket uses barcodes and barcode scanners at every checkout. Explain how the check digit on a barcode helps to maintain data accuracy, and discuss what would happen if the check digit was not present.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear explanation that the check digit is a mathematically calculated digit appended to the barcode; when a barcode is scanned the system recalculates the digit from the other numbers and compares it to the scanned value — a mismatch signals a scanning error. Discussion of consequences without check digit: a misread barcode digit would go undetected and the wrong product/price would be recorded; customers could be overcharged or undercharged; stock control data would be corrupted; the error would only be discovered much later when manual audits or customer complaints arise. Also effective at catching transposition errors.
Secure (3-4 marks): Check digit explained at a basic level with some consequence discussed.
Developing (2 marks): Describes that check digit detects errors but without sufficient explanation or consequences.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which validation check ensures that a required field such as a surname or email address has not been left empty?
Which of the following is a verification technique used to check that data has been entered correctly?
A _____ check confirms that a number entered into a field falls within acceptable limits — for example, an exam score must be between 0 and 100.
_____ is an automated check by the computer that data is reasonable and in the correct format, while _____ confirms that data has been copied accurately from a source.
Match each data capture method to the situation where it is most commonly used.
right: Reads product codes on items at a supermarket checkout
Automatically records environmental readings such as temperature without human input
Detects pencil marks on multiple-choice exam answer sheets

glossary_terms.definition: The methods and devices used to collect raw data and enter it into a computer system for processing.
An automated check performed by a computer to ensure that data entered into a field is reasonable, sensible and in the correct format — though it cannot confirm the data is factually correct.
A process of checking that data has been transferred from one place to another accurately and without change — confirming the copy matches the source.
An extra digit added to a code, calculated mathematically from the other digits, used to detect keying or scanning errors when the code is re-entered or scanned.
A mistake that occurs when data is copied from one location or format to another, such as mistyping a digit or swapping two characters.

lessons.title: Networks and Connectivity
lessons.description: LANs, WANs, network topologies, protocols, cloud computing, and wired and wireless connectivity methods explained.
lessons.content_html:
Networks: LAN and WAN

A Local Area Network (LAN) connects computers and devices within a small, defined area — typically a single building, school, hospital or office campus. All the hardware is usually owned and managed by the organisation itself. A Wide Area Network (WAN) connects devices across much larger geographical distances — cities, countries or even continents. The internet is the largest example of a WAN. Unlike a LAN, a WAN typically uses infrastructure owned and managed by third-party telecommunications companies, and the organisation leases access to those connections. The main differences to know are: LANs cover a small area and are owned by the organisation; WANs cover a large area and rely on external infrastructure.

Protocols

Protocols are the agreed rules and standards that control how data is sent, received and formatted across a network. Without protocols, devices from different manufacturers would be unable to communicate. The most important protocol suite is TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol), which governs how data is broken into packets, addressed and reassembled at the destination. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) governs how web pages are requested and delivered; HTTPS is its secure, encrypted version. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used to transfer files between computers. Email relies on protocols such as SMTP (for sending) and POP3 or IMAP (for receiving). Protocols allow a smartphone made in South Korea, a laptop running software from the USA, and a server hosted in the UK to exchange data seamlessly.

Internet, Intranet and Extranet

The internet is a global public network accessible to anyone — the network of all networks. An intranet is a private network that looks and works like the internet but is accessible only to people within a specific organisation, such as a company's employees. It might host internal documents, HR policies and staff forums. An extranet extends an intranet to give controlled, limited access to selected external users — for example, a supplier might be given access to a retailer's stock management system through an extranet, but cannot access the rest of the intranet. The key distinction is access: internet = public; intranet = private, internal; extranet = private, selectively external.

Network Topologies

A network topology describes how devices are physically or logically arranged and connected. There are three topologies to know. In a bus topology, all devices are connected to a single central cable called the backbone or bus. Data sent by one device travels along the bus in both directions until it reaches the intended recipient. Bus networks are cheap to install but if the backbone cable fails the whole network fails, and performance degrades as more devices are added because all devices share the same cable. In a star topology, every device connects to a central hub or switch. All data passes through the central device. Star networks are reliable because a single device failure does not affect others; they are easy to manage and fast because each device has a dedicated connection to the hub. The main disadvantage is that if the central hub or switch fails, the entire network goes down, and more cable is required than in a bus topology. In a ring topology, devices are connected in a loop and data travels in one direction around the ring, passing through each device until it reaches the correct destination. Ring networks avoid data collisions (since data travels in one direction), but if any single connection or device in the ring fails, the whole network is affected.

Key Fact

Three network topologies: bus (single shared cable — cheap but fragile), star (all connect to a central hub — reliable per device but hub is a single point of failure), ring (loop of devices — no collisions but one break stops everything).

Devices Within a Network

Several hardware devices make a network function. A router directs (routes) data packets between networks — it is what connects your home LAN to the wider internet. A switch connects multiple devices within a LAN and directs data only to the device it is intended for, reducing unnecessary traffic. A hub is an older, less intelligent version of a switch that broadcasts data to all connected devices. A modem converts digital computer signals into a form that can travel over telephone or cable lines (and converts incoming signals back). A network interface card (NIC) is the hardware component inside each device that allows it to connect to a network. Wireless Access Points (WAPs) allow Wi-Fi-enabled devices to connect to a wired network wirelessly.

How Data Is Transferred and Threats to Data Transfer

When data travels across a network it is divided into small chunks called packets. Each packet contains the data payload, the destination address, the source address and a sequence number so that packets can be reassembled in the correct order at the other end, even if they travelled by different routes. Packet switching allows networks to be more efficient because different packets can take different routes depending on congestion.

One significant threat to data in transit is packet sniffing. A packet sniffer is software (or hardware) that intercepts and reads packets as they travel across a network. On an unencrypted network, a malicious user running a packet sniffer can read usernames, passwords, email contents and financial data in plain text. Encryption (such as HTTPS) protects against packet sniffing by scrambling the data so that even if packets are intercepted, they cannot be read without the decryption key. Other threats include man-in-the-middle attacks and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks that flood a network with traffic to overwhelm it.

Cloud Computing versus In-house Servers

Cloud computing means storing data and running applications on remote servers accessed over the internet, rather than on hardware physically located in an organisation's own building. Benefits include: no need to buy and maintain expensive server hardware; storage can scale up or down as needed; data is accessible from anywhere with an internet connection; the cloud provider handles backups, security updates and maintenance. Drawbacks include: dependence on a reliable internet connection; ongoing subscription costs; data is held by a third party (raising questions about privacy and legal jurisdiction); potential security risks if the cloud provider is breached. In-house servers give the organisation full physical control over its hardware and data, compliance with strict data regulations is easier to demonstrate, and there is no reliance on internet connectivity for internal systems. The trade-off is higher upfront cost, the need for specialist IT staff to maintain the hardware, and limited scalability.

Key Fact

Cloud computing: scalable, accessible anywhere, no maintenance burden, but requires internet access and data is held by a third party. In-house servers: full control, no internet dependency, easier regulatory compliance, but expensive to buy and maintain.

Connectivity Methods

Devices connect to networks through a wide range of methods. Short-range wireless connections include: 802.11 (Wi-Fi) — the standard for wireless local networking, covering a building or campus; Bluetooth — connects devices like headphones and keyboards up to around 10 metres; NFC (Near-Field Communication) — works within a few centimetres for contactless payments; RFID — uses radio waves to identify tagged objects, used in library tracking and stock management. Medium-range wireless connections include mobile data networks: 3G (basic browsing), 4G (video streaming on smartphones) and 5G (very high speeds and low latency). Long-range wireless methods include: microwave transmission — line-of-sight radio signals between fixed tower antennas; satellite — data relayed via an orbiting satellite, enabling remote-area connectivity though with higher latency. Wired connections include: Ethernet — the standard for wired LANs using twisted-pair copper cable; USB-C — a reversible connector with fast speeds and higher power delivery, standard on modern laptops and smartphones; older USB-A and Micro USB connectors are still widely found on legacy devices.

Both NFC and Bluetooth are short-range wireless technologies, but they work at very different distances and serve different purposes. NFC works only within a few centimetres — you must almost touch two NFC-enabled devices together. It is designed for quick, spontaneous interactions: tapping your phone to pay at a checkout, or touching your bus pass to a reader. The connection happens in milliseconds and requires no pairing or setup. Bluetooth works at distances up to around 10 metres and requires a one-time pairing between devices. It is designed for continuous, sustained connections: wireless headphones, a keyboard connected to a laptop, or a smartwatch syncing with a phone. Because NFC is so close-range, it is inherently more secure for payment — it is very difficult for an attacker to intercept a signal that only works at a distance of a few centimetres.

When data travels across a network it is broken into packets. On a shared or poorly secured network — such as an open public Wi-Fi hotspot — any device on the same network can potentially intercept those packets using freely available packet-sniffer software. If the data is unencrypted, the attacker reads the contents directly: login credentials, credit card numbers, private messages. Encryption scrambles the data before transmission using a mathematical algorithm and a key. Even if the attacker captures the packets, all they see is meaningless ciphertext. Only the intended recipient, with the correct decryption key, can read the original data. HTTPS (which you see in your browser's address bar on secure websites) uses TLS encryption to protect web traffic from packet sniffing. Using a VPN (Virtual Private Network) also encrypts all outgoing traffic, providing protection even on unsecured public networks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Network questions frequently ask you to compare topologies or connectivity methods for a specific scenario — always relate your answer to the context given. If asked about threats to data transfer, name packet sniffing specifically and explain how encryption mitigates it — vague answers like "hackers could steal the data" will not reach the higher mark bands. For connectivity methods, the exam may give you a scenario (e.g. a nurse using a tablet on a hospital ward, or a delivery driver in a rural area) and ask which method is most appropriate — think through range, speed, whether infrastructure exists, and cost. Know that NFC is contact-range, Bluetooth is room-range, Wi-Fi is building-range, 4G/5G is city/country-range and satellite works globally.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A LAN covers a small area owned by the organisation; a WAN covers a large geographical area using third-party infrastructure. The internet is the largest WAN.
  • Protocols are agreed rules that allow different devices to communicate — TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS, FTP and SMTP/POP3 are examples.
  • Internet = public; intranet = private internal network; extranet = private network with selective external access.
  • Three topologies: bus (single cable — cheap but fragile), star (hub at centre — reliable per device), ring (loop — no collisions but one failure breaks everything).
  • Packet sniffing intercepts unencrypted data in transit; HTTPS encryption defends against it.
  • Cloud computing offers scalability and remote access; in-house servers offer control and independence from internet connectivity.
  • Connectivity methods: short-range (802.11 Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, NFC, RFID), medium-range (3G/4G/5G), long-range (microwave, satellite), wired (Ethernet, USB, Micro USB, USB-C).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
A) A network that connects devices within a single school building
B) A network that connects devices across large geographical distances using external infrastructure
C) A private network accessible only to employees within one organisation
D) A network topology where all devices connect to a central hub
practice_questions.marks: B) A network that connects devices across large geographical distances using external infrastructure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct differences: LAN covers a small/local area vs WAN covers a large/wide geographical area; LAN hardware is owned by the organisation vs WAN uses leased third-party infrastructure; LANs are typically faster and cheaper to run than WANs; LANs are more secure as they are physically confined to one site. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a protocol is and why protocols are important in computer networks.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): a protocol is a set of agreed rules and standards governing how data is formatted, transmitted and received across a network. Why important (2 marks): without protocols, devices from different manufacturers could not communicate (1 mark); protocols ensure all devices on a network follow the same rules so data is sent and received reliably, regardless of device or operating system (1 mark for a developed explanation). Named example adds quality but is not required for full marks. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school is setting up a new computer network in its IT suite. Compare a star topology and a bus topology, identifying one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
practice_questions.marks: Star topology advantage (1 mark): if one device fails it does not affect the rest of the network / each device has a dedicated connection to the hub so performance is better. Star topology disadvantage (1 mark): if the central hub or switch fails the entire network goes down / requires more cable than a bus topology. Bus topology advantage (1 mark): cheaper to install as less cable is needed / easy to add devices to the backbone. Bus topology disadvantage (1 mark): if the backbone cable fails the entire network fails / performance degrades as more devices are added. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what packet sniffing is and describe one way an organisation can protect its data from this threat.
practice_questions.marks: Packet sniffing explanation (2 marks): software or hardware that intercepts and reads data packets as they travel across a network (1); on an unencrypted network the attacker can read sensitive information such as usernames, passwords and financial data in plain text (1). Protection method (2 marks): using encryption such as HTTPS / TLS (1) scrambles the data so that intercepted packets cannot be read without the decryption key (1). Other valid methods: VPN, using a secured/encrypted Wi-Fi network. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A rural village has no mobile phone signal and no cable broadband infrastructure. A local business needs reliable internet access to run its online shop.

Discuss which connectivity method or methods would be most suitable for this business, considering the advantages and disadvantages of each option.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Identifies satellite communication as the primary viable option given the absence of mobile and cable infrastructure. Advantages of satellite: works anywhere with a clear view of the sky, no reliance on ground infrastructure, can support broadband speeds with modern low-Earth orbit satellites. Disadvantages: higher latency with traditional geostationary satellites (which may affect real-time processes); equipment costs; monthly subscription. Considers whether 3G/4G/5G might be possible if partial signal exists with a booster. Microwave could work if the business has line-of-sight to a tower and the infrastructure is available. Wired Ethernet connects internal devices on site but cannot solve the last-mile connectivity problem. A substantiated recommendation is made (e.g. satellite is the only realistic option in this scenario, and low-Earth orbit satellite services are increasingly viable for rural businesses). Discusses trade-off between performance and cost.
Secure (5-6 marks): Satellite identified and discussed with advantages and disadvantages; at least one other method considered; recommendation attempted.
Developing (3-4 marks): One or two relevant methods identified but analysis is limited.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic relevant point with no development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which network topology connects all devices to a single shared backbone cable, making the whole network vulnerable if that cable fails?

right: Long-range wireless — works globally, including remote areas
Medium-range wireless — covers cities and regions via mobile cell towers
Short-range wireless — typically works up to around 10 metres

glossary_terms.definition: A network that connects computers and devices within a limited geographical area such as a single building, school or office site.
A network that connects computers and devices across large geographical areas, potentially spanning cities, countries or continents, often using leased telecommunication lines.
A set of agreed rules and standards that govern how data is formatted, transmitted and received across a network, ensuring different devices can communicate reliably.
A short-range wireless standard for connecting devices over distances up to about 10 metres, commonly used for headphones, keyboards and file transfer between phones.
The interception and reading of data packets travelling across a network, using specialist software, which can expose unencrypted data to unauthorised users.
